outputs.L2:
Before motherhood existed for you, I already recognized you: salamander-shaped, drifting through fluid, a monstrous mind suspended there. I knew you when every bond began and ended within you, before any past offered a place to fasten yourself, like a shellfish clinging to nothing. There was no metallic nourishment, no vessel to carry you elsewhere; you remained fixed, moving only enough to keep the question beneath you.

I knew you as vision mixed with drink, your consciousness as vacant as the heavens—a root belonging neither to earth nor placenta. No severing had stained you crimson; suffering had not yet startled you. A single dreadful eye occupied the middle of your skull, opened toward the revolving darkness while the stars winked with feline light.

Together we floated through champagne’s final drops before mother’s milk became known to us. We inhabited the wardrobe’s darkness, the parasitic seal tightening around the mark of our thumbs; our blurred traces appeared inside a book colored yellow. My son, we were silent, unsawn timber—oak with no mouth—and courage came to us before remembrance did.
outputs.L3:
The speaker claims to have known the son even before birth, when he was still a primitive and isolated being, without history, identity, or any clear sense of self. In that early state, the son existed without external support, movement, or connection to the world. He seemed suspended in uncertainty, waiting silently for life to begin.

Before he encountered the pain of birth, he perceived the darkness of night and the stars through a single, newly awakened consciousness. During this hidden period, the speaker and the son shared an intimate, almost parasitic existence, preceding nourishment, individuality, and memory. They had not yet become separate beings with distinct experiences or identities. Instead, they remained unformed and undivided, like uncut oak: silent, complete, and courageous in the timeless moment before memory began.
outputs.L4:
The speaker addresses her son through surreal, prenatal imagery, imagining a time before birth when neither of them possessed a separate identity. In this imagined state, they existed together before motherhood had defined her and before the child had acquired a body, a name, or a personal history. Their connection appears complete and instinctive: they are not yet divided into parent and child, self and other, but belong to a primal realm beyond ordinary time and memory.

This vision gives their shared origin a sense of innocence and courage. Before entering the world, they seem untouched by fear, loss, or the burdens of experience. Birth, however, ends that unity. It creates two distinct bodies and establishes the relationship between mother and son, but it also introduces distance, vulnerability, and the possibility of suffering. The very event that gives the child an individual life therefore becomes a form of separation.

Memory deepens this division. Once personal history begins, each person accumulates experiences that the other cannot fully share. The mother can imagine their earlier unity, but she cannot recover it; the son, meanwhile, cannot consciously remember it at all. The poem thus presents identity as both necessary and painful. To become an individual is to gain a self, yet it is also to lose the undivided belonging that existed before birth. Through its dreamlike imagery, the poem transforms motherhood into a meditation on origins, suggesting that love is shaped not only by intimacy but also by the irreversible separation between one life and another.
outputs.L5:
**I Knew You**

I knew you before I learned the shape of your silence—before I understood how your eyes could hold an entire storm without letting a single drop fall. You arrived like a familiar song playing in a distant room, and something in me recognized the melody.

Maybe we had met in another life, under another sky. Maybe some people simply carry a sense of home wherever they go.

I knew you in the way you paused before saying goodbye, as if leaving was never what you truly wanted. I knew you in every unfinished sentence, every hidden smile, every moment you pretended not to care.

And when the years pulled us in different directions, I still found traces of you everywhere: in quiet mornings, in old photographs, in songs I could no longer hear without remembering.

Perhaps I do not know you now. Time changes people; distance rewrites them. But once, for one bright and fleeting moment, I knew you.

And somehow, that was enough.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in lowercase from a parent addressing a son, imagining their bond before birth, memory, and language, with unsettling embryonic and cosmic imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
son, before you were born, i carried your silence like a second skeleton. you slept in the red astronomy beneath my ribs, curled around your own small thunder, while the moon pressed its blind face to the window.

perhaps we knew each other earlier, before blood learned its alphabet. perhaps you were a pale animal drifting through the first ocean, and i was the salt that entered your unfinished mouth. your fingers opened like five questions. your eyes, still sealed, watched the dark invent us.

i remember what cannot be remembered: the cord between us humming with dead stars, each pulse translating the void. you spoke without a tongue. i answered without a name. our language was wet and circular, made of doors that led only deeper into the body.

then birth divided the sentence.

you arrived blue with distance, carrying a little universe of afterbirth and terror. they placed you against me, and your heart knocked from the other side of matter. son, even now, when you call me, i hear that first impossible voice—the black seed of speech splitting open, the cosmos whispering through its teeth.

one day memory will misplace us. my face will loosen in your mind; your childhood will float away like a ruined planet. but somewhere beneath language, beneath bone, we will remain: two shadows sharing one warm cave, listening as the unborn stars chew slowly through the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental monologue that begins “i knew you before you had a mother” and explores prenatal existence through images of water, eyes, boats, metal, champagne, breastmilk, and oak.
counterfactuals.output:
i knew you before you had a mother

before the word *mother* buttoned its white coat  
over the animal dark, before anyone lifted  
a champagne glass and called your absence  
a future.

You were water rehearsing a body.

You were the small inland sea where eyes  
floated shut, not blind, only unwilling  
to choose a world. I watched them dream  
their blueprints: two black boats moored  
under translucent weather, waiting  
for the face to rise around them.

Do you remember the crossing?

No. Memory had not yet been invented.  
Still, you traveled—passenger and vessel,  
cargo and tide—your spine a keel,  
your ribs becoming oars in pairs.  
Somewhere beyond the red harbor  
metal instruments slept in drawers,  
cold moons with sharpened edges.  
Somewhere a clock kept striking  
its little hammer against the century.

But inside, no clocks.

Only water licking water.  
Only the pulse, that blind mechanic,  
testing the engine with a wet thumb.  
Only your mouth learning hunger  
from the dark, opening and closing  
around the rumor of breastmilk—  
that white river not yet poured,  
that sweetness waiting in another body  
like snow waiting inside a cloud.

They drank champagne for you  
before you could swallow. Gold weather  
climbed the glasses. Bubbles rose  
like souls reconsidering heaven.  
Everyone said *to the child*,  
and the crystal rang, and you turned  
in your private ocean, startled  
by a celebration you could not hear.

Listen: even then the world was hardening.

Iron in the blood. Silver in the tray.  
A metal name being forged for you,  
letter by letter, beneath a tongue  
you had not met. They would fasten it  
to your ankle, your schoolbooks, your debts.  
They would call it yours.

But I knew you when you were nameless.

I knew the soft architecture,  
the unfinished doors of your hands,  
the eyes sealed like envelopes  
addressed to light. I knew the boat  
before it touched air, before the hull  
cried out against the shore.

And your mother—she was not yet mother.  
She was oak under lightning,  
oak full of sap and hidden rings,  
standing in a field no one else could enter.  
You grew in her as a tree grows  
around a nail: taking the metal inward,  
making room, making grain,  
turning the wound into a center.

Later, they placed you on her chest.

The boats opened.

The eyes took on weather.  
The mouth found breastmilk  
and believed, for one bright instant,  
that the world had always been white,  
warm, inexhaustible.

But I remember otherwise.

I remember you as water  
holding its breath inside water.  
I remember the oak door before the house,  
the champagne before the thirst,  
the metal before the scar.

I remember you before *before*  
had somewhere to stand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: Before the first thought blistered open, they knew each other as pressure, as salt, as two pale organs turning in the black amnion of heaven—no names, no faces, only cilia tasting starlight, only bone buds ringing beneath unfinished skin. Around them the galaxies molted. Suns hung like infected eyes. They drifted through the great body before consciousness, where time was a wet nerve and every future twitched inside it; touching without hands, speaking through spasms, through the soft percussion of hearts not yet enclosed. Then came the wound of I. Then the skull’s bright prison, the mouth filling with history, the terrible separation into two. Yet somewhere beneath language, beneath the scar tissue of identity, they remembered the dark that had carried them together—and knew they had been brave before memory.

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a mother speaking to her unborn or newborn son across time. Produce a strange, visceral passage in which fetus, parasite, root, barnacle, animal, and tree imagery blur together.
counterfactuals.output:
My son, before you had a face you were a pale root nosing through me, blind and thirsty. You drank the dark behind my organs. You fastened yourself beneath my heart like a barnacle to the red hull of a ship, and while I slept you built your little animal from salt, marrow, and stolen weather.

I spoke to you then, though you had no ears—only the soft gills of becoming. I said: Hold fast, small parasite, small seed with teeth. Let my blood be your river. Let my spine be the tree you climb in darkness. You answered by turning, a hooked fish in the black pond of me, and my whole body rang like timber struck by an axe.

Years from now, when your hands are larger than mine, I will still feel you rooted there: a ghost-knot under the bark, a hoofbeat in an empty stable. You will call me Mother as if I had not once been earth, carcass, nest; as if you had not crawled out of my torn season slick as a seal and furious as fire.

But listen—whether you are still curled inside me or already walking away: the cord is never cut cleanly. It becomes a vine too thin to see. It loops through houses, graves, oceans. At its far end I am always bleeding you into the world, and you are always feeding, mouth bright with first light, my beautiful wound, my branch that learned to run.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
